source:
Backyard Monsters is one of the most underappreciated strategy games ever made. It combined Clash of Clans, Factorio, tower defense, RTS, and idle progression years before most mobile games. The core loop was: build a monster base, gather resources, research new monsters, attack other players, and defend your own base while upgrades continued in real time.
I actually think a Roblox spiritual successor could be bigger than the original, because Roblox solves many of the social and multiplayer limitations that Facebook games had.

The Fantasy
You're not building a town.
You're growing a monster civilization hidden inside a suburban backyard.
Imagine:
 • gigantic mushrooms
 • monster nests
 • slime rivers
 • tree forts
 • toy blocks
 • abandoned bicycles
 • sprinklers become rivers
 • garden hoses become bridges
 • sandbox becomes a desert biome
The world feels gigantic because you're tiny.

Idle Progression

Enough idle to respect players' time, but not so much that active play feels unnecessary.

Roblox-Specific Improvements
This is where a clone can become something much larger.
Instead of every player living in an isolated instance, imagine an entire persistent neighborhood server with 20-40 players.
Each player owns one backyard, but everyone can:
 • Walk to neighboring yards.
 • Watch live attacks.
 • Trade monster DNA.
 • Visit alliance fortresses.
 • Participate in neighborhood events (like defending against a giant cat invading multiple bases).
This makes the world feel alive in a way the original never could.

Technical Architecture

Server
├── Persistent World
├── Base Simulation
├── Resource Production
├── Combat Engine
├── Pathfinding
├── AI Behavior Trees
├── Research System
├── Alliance System
├── Matchmaking
├── Economy
└── Live Events

Client
├── Building Mode
├── RTS Controls
├── Combat VFX
├── Monster Animation
├── UI
├── Camera
└── Audio

Each player's base is an independently simulated "island" within the larger neighborhood, allowing efficient server performance while still supporting social interactions and live events.

Long-Term Retention
The best strategy games always have goals on multiple timescales:
 • 5-minute session: Collect resources, queue upgrades, check breeding results, attack one nearby base.
 • 30-minute session: Explore a new biome, defeat a boss, redesign your defenses, experiment with a new army composition.
 • Weekly goal: Complete alliance events, unlock a new monster family, climb ranked PvP, finish research branches.
 • Monthly goal: Earn limited seasonal monsters, evolve Ancient monsters, upgrade your fortress, and compete for neighborhood dominance.
The original Backyard Monsters proved that combining base building, asynchronous PvP, and long-term progression was compelling. A modern Roblox version could push that much further by emphasizing collectible monsters with unique AI, exploration beyond the home base, cooperative neighborhood gameplay, and a living world that changes through seasonal events rather than simply recreating the original formula.

image_prompt.text: Broad buildable backyard ground radiating out from the Monster Heart, where nests, extractors, walls and turrets are placed by proximity rather than on a grid
The Monster Heart at the centre of the base, the structure everything else branches from and the thing raiders come to break
Raised ground - stacked toy blocks, tree-fort platforms, the lip of the sandbox - giving long-range monsters a placement advantage
Tall grass blades and oversized trees that block sight lines across the yard
Barriers at the yard's edge opening onto the neighbourhood, park, sewer and later world tiers
Player-built defences worked into the backyard theme: spike traps, acid pools, Tesla towers, slime launchers, giant Venus flytraps, laser garden gnomes
A base building set of monster nests, resource extractors, storages, laboratories, breeding caves and spell towers, each readable at several upgrade tiers
Oversized backyard objects as terrain: garden hoses as bridges, sprinklers as rivers, abandoned bicycles, broken toys, the sandbox as a desert

layout_placement.text: The Monster Heart as the base's health pool, defensible from every direction
Thematic resource sites across the yard - Mush, Goo, Bones, Electricity from backyard electronics, Scrap from broken toys
Terrain modifier volumes: mud that traps, sprinkler-flooded ground that slows, tall grass that hides units
Deployment ground around the outside of an enemy base where a raiding player drops their monster squad
Boss spawn sites in the outer yard for the garden snake, lawn mower, cat and raccoon

notes: The prompt is a full systems design document; only the base, its terrain and the outer world tiers are layout concerns and the rest was let go.

The world map (backyard to neighbourhood to park to sewer to school to construction site to shopping centre to national forest) cannot be one framed image - it needs a separate-map route per tier, which no picked option carries.
Base defense elements from a second Strategy preset were not taken; the RTS preset's open terrain plus free placement already expresses the base.
Close call with Simulation (tycoon plot, idle production); Strategy chosen because the loop ends in attacking and defending bases.

open_questions.ask: Should we build one backyard base first, or the whole neighbourhood world map? Eight expanding world tiers will not fit in a single top-down image, so they would be separate maps.
Are the neighbouring players' yards inside the same map as yours, or separate instances you travel to?

theme: Miniature suburban backyard - oversized garden and toy objects at insect scale, stylized and slightly grotesque

coverage_missing.ask: One backyard, or the whole neighbourhood? The eight world tiers cannot share one frame.
Is every player's yard in one shared map, or does each base sit in its own instance with a hub between them?
How stylized should the backyard read - bright toy-box colours, or grimy realistic suburbia seen from ant height?
What ends a raid - destroying the Monster Heart, a timer, a percentage of the base flattened?

answers.ask: Should we build one backyard base first, or the whole neighbourhood world map? Eight expanding world tiers will not fit in a single top-down image, so they would be separate maps.
answers.answer: Build one backyard base first as the playable vertical slice. The wider world map and its expanding tiers can come later as separate maps.

answers.ask: Are the neighbouring players' yards inside the same map as yours, or separate instances you travel to?
answers.answer: Neighbouring players' yards should be separate instances you travel to for scouting and raids, keeping each base focused and readable.
